Field surveys of the Striped mojarra (Eugerres plumieri) in coastal lagoons of the southwestern Gulf of Mexico indicate that individuals typically reach sexual maturity at a standard length of 22 centimeters [Lp = 22 centimeters], a size that corresponds to the onset of gonadal recrudescence in this species. Populations inhabiting these warm, brackish environments experience a spawning season that extends from late spring through early autumn, during which gravid females are routinely captured. The standard length at puberty represents a useful benchmark for fisheries management, as it marks the transition from the juvenile phase to the reproductively active adult stock. In this species, individuals that have not yet attained this length are considered sexually immature and do not contribute to annual recruitment. Comparative data from several gerreid species suggest that the size at first maturation in Eugerres plumieri is intermediate relative to congeners of similar maximum body size, reflecting a life-history strategy that balances early reproductive output with continued somatic growth. The seasonal timing of spawning appears to be linked to the annual cycle of salinity and temperature in the lagoon systems, with peak spawning activity coinciding with the onset of the rainy season.

At a stable water temperature of 26.9 °C [T = 26.9 °C], the maximum reproductive rate for the Striped mojarra has been estimated from laboratory observations of captive breeders, revealing that individual females produce approximately 2613 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 2613 eggs per spawning event] and spawn roughly once per day [F_R_i = spawn roughly once per day] during the peak of the reproductive season. This exceptionally high daily fecundity is consistent with a batch-spawning strategy, whereby a single female releases multiple clutches over the course of several weeks, thereby maximizing the number of propagules entering the planktonic larval pool. The reproductive output is strongly temperature-dependent, and the values recorded at 26.9 °C likely represent near-optimal conditions for gametogenesis and oviposition in this subtropical species. At lower temperatures, the interval between successive spawning events lengthens considerably, reducing the overall seasonal fecundity. These findings underscore the importance of thermal regime in shaping the reproductive phenology of coastal marine fishes.

The hatchlings of Eugerres plumieri emerge from their pelagic eggs at a remarkably small size, with the wet weight at birth estimated at approximately 0.0000655 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0000655 grams], a value typical of marine teleosts that produce numerous, tiny propagules. This initial mass is derived from the diameter of the yolksac larva, which measures roughly half a millimeter across at the moment of eclosion, following an incubation period that lasts less than 24 hours in warm waters. The newly emerged prolarvae are entirely lecithotrophic, relying on their endogenous yolk reserves for the first few days of life before the mouth opens and exogenous feeding commences. During this yolk-dependent phase, the larva undergoes rapid morphological differentiation, including the development of the retinal pigments necessary for prey detection. The transition to exotrophic feeding is a critical bottleneck in the early life history, and the small size at birth imposes a high risk of starvation if suitable planktonic prey is not abundant. This energy-poor start to life is compensated for by the sheer numerical output of eggs produced by each spawning female.

As the juvenile fish grow and approach their maximum body size, the asymptotic wet weight recorded in the adult population reaches 1057 grams [Wwi = 1057 grams], a substantial mass that is achieved after several years of continuous feeding in the productive estuarine environment, a value that is among the highest recorded for the genus Eugerres and reflects the high productivity of the coastal lagoon habitats where this species feeds primarily on benthic invertebrates. This ultimate wet weight corresponds to a standard length of approximately 40 centimeters [Li = approximately 40 centimeters], which represents the largest size class routinely observed in field samples from the Gulf coast. The length-weight relationship for this species follows a slightly positive allometric pattern, indicating that larger individuals are proportionally heavier for their length. Sexual dimorphism in ultimate size is minimal, although gravid females tend to be slightly heavier due to the mass of the developing ovaries. The attainment of this asymptotic mass marks the end of the rapid growth phase and the onset of a period in which most available energy is directed toward reproductive effort rather than somatic increase. In the lagoon ecosystems where this species predominates, individuals exceeding 40 centimeters are uncommon, likely because of size-selective pressure from commercial and artisanal fisheries that target the largest specimens.

The maximum lifespan of Eugerres plumieri has been estimated at approximately 3100 days [am = approximately 3100 days] under the thermal conditions typical of its natural habitat, which averages 26.9 °C [T = 26.9 °C] throughout much of the year, a lifespan that places it among the longer-lived gerreids and is consistent with the slow growth rates observed in subtropical lagoon populations. This longevity, roughly equivalent to eight and a half years, places the Striped mojarra among the longer-lived members of the Gerreidae, a family generally characterized by moderately fast life histories. At the onset of puberty, individuals weigh approximately 173 grams [Wwp = approximately 173 grams], a mass that represents a considerable investment of somatic tissue prior to the initiation of reproductive activity. The gap between the wet weight at puberty and the ultimate wet weight of over one kilogram underscores the substantial scope for post-maturation growth in this species. Senescence in wild populations is poorly documented, but captive individuals typically exhibit a gradual decline in fecundity and body condition beyond the sixth year of life. The interplay between a relatively high maximum reproductive output and a long reproductive lifespan suggests that Striped mojarra populations are resilient to moderate fishing pressure, provided that the spawning stock is not depleted below critical thresholds.
